questions.first: I regret not visiting my grandmother more often before she passed away.
questions.after: more often before she passed away.
questions.explanation: 'Wish' followed by the past perfect expresses regret about something in the past that cannot now be changed.

questions.first: If it hadn't been for her quick thinking, the situation could have been far worse.
questions.after: her quick thinking, the situation could have been far worse.
questions.explanation: 'Were it not for' is a formal inverted conditional structure meaning 'if it were not for', used instead of 'if' to introduce the one factor that prevented a worse outcome.

questions.first: The company was about to go bankrupt when a new investor stepped in.
questions.after: bankruptcy when a new investor stepped in.
questions.explanation: 'Be on the verge of' is a fixed idiom meaning 'be about to', used here to describe how close the company came to bankruptcy.

questions.first: She had only just arrived when the phone rang.
questions.after: arrived when the phone rang.
questions.explanation: 'Hardly' at the start of a sentence triggers inversion of the subject and auxiliary ('hardly had she arrived'), a formal structure for saying one thing happened immediately after another.

questions.first: Nobody was remotely surprised when the firm announced record profits.
questions.after: to anyone who had followed its recent growth.
questions.explanation: 'Come as no surprise' is a fixed idiom meaning 'be entirely expected', shifting the focus from the people (who were not surprised) to the profits themselves.

questions.first: Her recovery after the accident was absolutely amazing.
questions.before: Her recovery after the accident was
questions.after: amazing.
questions.explanation: 'Nothing short of' is a fixed idiom used before an adjective to intensify it, meaning 'absolutely' or 'no less than'.

questions.first: "Don't touch that wire," the electrician said to the apprentice.
questions.after: touch that wire.
questions.explanation: A reported negative imperative is formed with 'tell someone not to do something'.

questions.first: It is highly likely that she missed the train, since she isn't answering her phone.
questions.after: the train, since she isn't answering her phone.
questions.explanation: 'Must have' plus the past participle expresses a confident deduction about the past.

questions.first: The company decided not to continue with the project because of rising costs.
questions.after: the project because of rising costs.
questions.explanation: 'Pull out of' is a phrasal verb meaning 'withdraw from', matching the meaning of 'not continue with'.

questions.first: I have absolutely no idea why she suddenly resigned.
questions.after: she suddenly resigned.
questions.explanation: 'Why on earth' is an idiomatic intensifier used to emphasise bewilderment about a reason.

questions.first: The judges did not consider her previous experience when making their decision.
questions.after: her previous experience when making their decision.
questions.explanation: 'Take into account' is a fixed phrase meaning 'consider' or 'allow for'.

questions.first: It last rained properly here in March.
questions.after: March.
questions.explanation: The present perfect negative with 'since' plus a point in time expresses that something has not happened from that point until now.

questions.first: She missed the flight because she forgot her passport at home.
questions.after: her passport at home, she wouldn't have missed the flight.
questions.explanation: The third conditional (if + past perfect, ... would have + past participle) describes an unreal past situation and its imagined result.

questions.first: They have to finish the report by Friday, according to the manager.
questions.after: by Friday, according to the manager.
questions.explanation: The passive form of an obligation ('has to be finished') shifts the focus from the people who must act to the report itself.

questions.first: This is easily the most interesting novel she has written.
questions.after: the most interesting novel she has written.
questions.explanation: 'By far' is a fixed intensifying phrase used before a superlative to emphasise the degree of difference.

questions.first: She resigned because she wanted to spend more time with her family.
questions.after: she resigned was that she wanted to spend more time with her family.
questions.explanation: 'The reason (why/that)' introduces a clause explaining a cause; the relative adverb 'why' or the relative pronoun 'that' can be included, or omitted altogether.

questions.first: The research team continued with their experiments despite the setback.
questions.after: despite the setback.
questions.explanation: 'Carry on with' is a phrasal verb meaning 'continue with', matching the meaning of the original sentence.

questions.first: My brother refused to give up during the negotiations, no matter how difficult they became.
questions.after: during the negotiations, no matter how difficult they became.
questions.explanation: 'Fight tooth and nail' is an idiom meaning to struggle fiercely and persistently for something.

questions.first: "I broke the vase," said Tom.
questions.after: the vase.
questions.explanation: 'Admit' is followed by a gerund directly or by 'to' plus a gerund; both forms report the confession correctly.

questions.first: I strongly advise you to see a doctor about that cough.
questions.after: see a doctor about that cough.
questions.explanation: 'Had better' is a fixed modal-like structure used to give strong advice or a warning.

questions.first: We don't have enough time to visit every museum, so we'll just see the main ones.
questions.after: of time, we'll just see the main museums.
questions.explanation: 'Running short of time' / 'being short of time' are fixed phrases meaning 'not having enough time left'; 'as/since we are short of time' expresses the same reason as a full clause.

questions.first: No matter the number of people who apply, only five positions are available.
questions.after: people apply, only five positions are available.
questions.explanation: 'However many' and 'no matter how many' are both fixed quantifying phrases meaning 'regardless of the number'.

questions.first: If there is a fire, please use the stairs, not the lift.
questions.after: a fire, please use the stairs, not the lift.
questions.explanation: 'In the event of' is a formal fixed phrase meaning 'if ... happens', used instead of 'if' in official instructions.

questions.first: Even if nothing else works out, I will still have the satisfaction of having tried.
questions.after: I will have the satisfaction of having tried.
questions.explanation: 'At least' is a fixed phrase meaning 'whatever else happens', introducing the one positive outcome that is guaranteed.
